Question_text: Fig. 1.1 shows the speed-time graph for a car. The cyclist leaves town A at time t = 0 and arrives at town B at t = 4.0 hours. At time t = 15s, the brakes are applied and the car comes to rest with uniform deceleration.
image: A speed-time graph titled 'Fig. 1.1'. The x-axis is 't/s' (time in seconds) ranging from 0 to 30. The y-axis is 'speed m/s' (speed in meters per second) ranging from 0 to 20. The graph shows a horizontal line at 10 m/s from t=0 to t=15s, indicating constant speed. From t=15s, the speed decreases linearly to 0 m/s at t=20s, indicating uniform deceleration. The grid lines are spaced every 5 units on both axes.

Parts.part_text: State the speed of the car just before the brakes are applied.
Explain what is meant by uniform deceleration.
A lorry travels at a constant speed of 18m/s for 15s. At time t = 15s, the brakes are applied and the lorry slows down with the same deceleration as the car.
On Fig. 1.1, draw the speed-time graph for the lorry.
Explain how your graph shows that, while braking, the lorry travels further than the car.

Question_text: Fig. 2.1 shows a sky-diver falling vertically downwards at terminal velocity. Arrows X and Y show the two main forces acting on the sky-diver.
image: A diagram titled 'Fig. 2.1' showing a sky-diver in a spread-eagle position, falling downwards. An upward pointing arrow labeled 'Y' originates from the sky-diver's center of mass, representing air resistance or drag. A downward pointing arrow labeled 'X' also originates from the sky-diver's center of mass, representing weight or gravitational force.

Parts.part_text: State the name of force X and the name of force Y.
Explain why force Y acts upwards.
When the sky-diver first started to fall, forces X and Y were unbalanced.
Describe and explain the effect of the unbalanced forces on the motion of the sky-diver.
State what happened to the size of force X and the size of force Y as the sky-diver fell and reached terminal velocity.

Question_text: Fig. 3.1 shows part of a small hydroelectric system that generates electricity from moving water.
image: A diagram titled 'Fig. 3.1' depicting a small hydroelectric system. Water flows through a horizontal 'pipe' which narrows at its end. Parts.part_text: Every minute, water with kinetic energy 14000J emerges from the pipe. The water turns a turbine that is connected to the generator. Half of the kinetic energy of the water is given to the generator.
Calculate the power input to the generator.
Suggest a reason why only some of the kinetic energy of the water is given to the generator.
Hydroelectric systems use sources of renewable energy.
State what is meant by renewable energy.
State one source of non-renewable energy.

Question_text: Water at a temperature of 16°C enters an ice-making machine and emerges as ice cubes at a temperature of -5°C. The melting point of ice is 0°C. specific heat capacity of liquid water = 4.2 × 10^3J/(kg°C) specific latent heat of fusion of water = 3.4 × 10^5J/kg specific heat capacity of ice = 2.1 x 10^3J/(kg °C)

Parts.part_text: Calculate the total energy removed from 1.0kg of water as it cools from 16°C, changes into ice, and then cools to –5°C.
Using ideas about molecules,
explain why energy is needed to change ice into water,
suggest why less energy is needed to change ice into water than to change the same mass of water into steam.

Question_text: Fig. 7.1 shows the structure of a circuit-breaker that uses an electromagnet. The circuit-breaker operates when the current is 10A.
image: A diagram titled 'Fig. 7.1' illustrating the structure of a circuit-breaker. It shows 'current in' flowing into a coil wrapped around an 'electromagnet'. Adjacent to the electromagnet is an 'iron bar' that is pivoted at its top end and has a 'spring' attached to its lower end. The iron bar is also connected to 'contacts' which are part of a 'copper bar'. The copper bar is pivoted and eventually leads to 'current out'. A 'fixed bar' is also shown. The setup is designed so that when the electromagnet is strong enough, it pulls the iron bar, causing the contacts to open and break the circuit.

Parts.part_text: On Fig. 7.1, mark with an arrow the force on the iron bar caused by the electromagnet.
Suggest one reason why the iron bar does not move when the current is less than 10A.
When the current is greater than 10A, the circuit-breaker stops the current. Explain what happens in the circuit-breaker when this occurs.
State and explain how the electromagnet can be altered so that the circuit-breaker stops the current at less than 10A.
